content: Uterine leiomyomas, also known as uterine fibroids, are benign tumors that arise from the smooth muscle of the uterus. Despite their benign nature, they can cause significant clinical symptoms, including excessive menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), anemia, and infertility. Treatment options include enucleation, which involves the removal of fibroids while preserving the uterus, and hysterectomy, which entails the complete removal of the uterus. Laser surgery, referred to as myolysis, is an emerging alternative to traditional surgical methods. Uterine leiomyomas originate in the myometrium and are categorized based on their location: submucosal (beneath the endometrium), intramural (within the uterine wall), and subserous (on the serosal surface of the uterus, sometimes pedunculated). Their growth is typically stimulated by estrogen and progesterone, and hormonal suppression can reduce their size. Leiomyomas are also the most common benign tumors of the esophagus, although they account for less than 1% of all esophageal neoplasms, with the majority being carcinomas. Most benign esophageal tumors are asymptomatic and remain undetected, but larger or strategically located tumors may cause symptoms. In the small intestine, leiomyomas are the most common benign tumors, with approximately 50% occurring in the jejunum and 31% in the ileum. Nearly half of these lesions are smaller than 5 centimeters in size. Gross pathological examination of uterine leiomyomas may reveal a solitary, large tumor that distorts the endometrial cavity, often creating a Y-shaped deformation by splaying and compressing the endometrium. Epidemiologically, uterine leiomyomas are five times more prevalent in African-American females compared to other populations. On computed tomography (CT) imaging, leiomyomas can be visualized, such as a leiomyoma located in the right broad ligament. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is particularly useful in differentiating leiomyomas from other conditions, such as adenomyosis, solid adnexal masses, focal myometrial contractions, and uterine leiomyosarcomas. Non-degenerated leiomyomas typically appear as well-circumscribed masses with homogeneously decreased signal intensity on T2-weighted images. In contrast, degenerated leiomyomas exhibit variable appearances on T2-weighted and contrast-enhanced images. For example, MRI may show large degenerating leiomyomas or a leiomyoma prolapsing into the endometrial canal. Ultrasound is a key diagnostic tool for identifying leiomyomas, with transabdominal or transvaginal ultrasonography being effective for detecting large submucosal and transmural myomas. Saline infusion sonography is particularly useful for identifying submucosal myomas. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) can also reveal submucosal leiomyomas. Medical therapy for leiomyomas often involves the use of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues for 3 to 6 months, which can reduce the size of the tumors by 60% to 70%. However, the fibroids typically regrow once the medication is discontinued. Surgical options include myomectomy, which is preferred for patients desiring to preserve fertility. Definitive treatment involves total abdominal or vaginal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.
